records.field_marks: Large, long-tailed cuckoo. Males are glossy bluish-black. Females are brownish with rufous streaks on the head, dark brown back/rump/wing coverts with white/buff spots, and whitish, heavily striped underparts. Young birds resemble males with black beaks.
records.habitat: A bird of light woodland and cultivation.
records.behavior: Brood parasite that lays eggs in the nests of crows and other hosts; adults are largely frugivorous.
records.similar_species: Forms a superspecies with black-billed and Pacific koels, which are sometimes treated as subspecies.
records.notes: Known for its vocalizations, especially the male's repeated 'koo-Ooo' song. Symbol in poetry and folklore.

records.field_marks: Glossy black bird with a distinctive wide fork to the tail. Adults often have a small white spot at the base of the gape. Sexes are indistinguishable in the field.
records.habitat: Common in open agricultural areas, light forest, savanna, fields, and urban habitats, perching conspicuously on bare perches or along power lines.
records.behavior: Known for aggressive behavior, dive-bombing larger birds like crows and birds of prey that invade its territory; also known for aerial insect capture.
records.similar_species: Iris is dark brown, unlike the crimson iris of the ashy drongo. Juveniles can be mistaken for the white-bellied drongo.
records.notes: Sometimes called 'king crow' due to its aggressive behavior. Attracts farmers to fields using artificial perches to control pest insects.

records.field_marks: Medium-sized bird of prey with angled wings and a distinctive forked tail. Generally dark plumage without rufous, paler head and neck, and pale brown underparts. Bill is black, legs are yellow.
records.habitat: Widely distributed through temperate and tropical parts of Eurasia, Australasia, Oceania, and Africa; some populations are migratory.
records.behavior: Opportunistic hunters and scavengers, often seen gliding in thermals searching for food; can be vociferous with a shrill whinnying call.
records.similar_species: Distinguished from red kites by slightly smaller size, less forked tail, and generally dark plumage. Bill is black, unlike the yellow-billed kite.
records.notes: Abundant species, though some populations have declined. Attracted to smoke and fires; known to spread wildfires. Can be bold around humans in urban areas.

records.field_marks: Brown body, black hooded head, and a bare yellow patch behind the eye. Bill and legs are bright yellow. White patch on outer primaries, white wing lining, and white tail tip.
records.habitat: Omnivorous open woodland bird that has adapted extremely well to urban environments.
records.behavior: Pairs for life, builds nests in holes in trees or walls, and is known for communal roosting.
records.similar_species: Sri Lankan subspecies (A. t. melanosternus) is darker with half-black/half-white primary coverts and a larger yellow cheek-patch.
records.notes: Considered one of the world's most invasive species, posing a threat to biodiversity and agriculture.

records.field_marks: Black plumage, low triangular casque, pink cheeks, and red patches of skin on a blue neck. Possesses large, powerful feet with dagger-like claws on the inner toe. Females are larger with longer casques and brighter bare skin.
records.habitat: Endemic to montane cloud forests and tropical rainforests.
records.behavior: A solitary bird that feeds on fruits, small animals, and insects, using its casque to sort through leaf litter.
records.similar_species: Smallest of the three extant cassowary species; shorter with a slightly smaller bill than southern and northern cassowaries.
records.notes: Casque does not glow under UV light, unlike other cassowaries.

records.field_marks: Soft, brown feathers, a long neck, and long legs. It is a tall, robust, bipedal runner.
records.size: Up to 1.9 m (6 ft 3 in) in height.
records.weight: Males lose significant weight during incubation.
records.habitat: Native ranges cover most of the Australian mainland.
records.behavior: Omnivorous, forages on plants and insects, can travel great distances and sprint at 48 km/h (30 mph).
records.similar_species: Third-tallest living bird after African ratites (ostrich, Somali ostrich).
records.notes: Flightless bird, only extant member of its genus. Important cultural icon of Australia.

records.field_marks: A small flightless bird, also known as little grey kiwi or kiwi pukupuku. It is the smallest of the five kiwi species.
records.size: Smallest of five kiwi species, about the size of a bantam.
records.habitat: Endemic to New Zealand, now mainly restricted to small offshore islands and mainland reserves protected by pest-exclusion fences.
records.notes: Was on the brink of extinction 100 years ago; rediscovered in the wild in 2025 after being considered extinct on the mainland since 1978.

records.habitat: Widespread in the northern two-thirds of the North Island of New Zealand.
records.notes: It is the most common kiwi species with about 35,000 remaining. Its eggs are among the largest relative to its body size.

records.field_marks: A large, stocky flightless bird, also known as the one-wattled, single-wattled, or golden-necked cassowary.
records.similar_species: One of three living cassowary species, alongside the dwarf cassowary and the southern cassowary.
records.notes: It is a member of the superorder Palaeognathae.

records.field_marks: Morphologically very similar to other members of the brown kiwi complex, making visual identification challenging.
records.habitat: Found in a restricted area of the Ōkārito forest on the West Coast of New Zealand's South Island.
records.similar_species: Morphologically very similar to other members of the brown kiwi complex.
records.notes: Described as new to science in 2003. Population of only about 600 birds.

records.field_marks: Largest living bird with a long neck and legs. Capable of high running speeds.
records.habitat: Native to certain areas of Africa and historically Arabia.
records.behavior: Lives in nomadic groups; lies flat to hide or runs when threatened; kicks if cornered.
records.similar_species: Somali ostrich is a distinct species.
records.notes: Lays the largest eggs of any living bird. Farmed for feathers, leather, and meat.

records.field_marks: Large flightless bird with a blue neck. Distinct species from the common ostrich.
records.habitat: Native to the Horn of Africa.
records.behavior: Somalis have partially domesticated some of these ostriches.
records.similar_species: Distinct species from the common ostrich.
records.notes: Also known as the blue-necked ostrich.

records.habitat: Found on South Island of New Zealand.
records.similar_species: Considered conspecific with the North Island brown kiwi until 2000, and still by some authorities.
records.notes: Also known as tokoeka or common kiwi.

records.field_marks: Large, flightless, mostly black bird with a prominent casque on its head and brightly colored wattles hanging from its neck.
records.habitat: Found in tropical rainforests, woodlands, and savannas.
records.behavior: Generally solitary and shy, but can be aggressive if threatened.
records.similar_species: Distinguished from other cassowaries by its two prominent wattles.
records.notes: Australian population is listed as Endangered.
